items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

entry.rationale: The question asks directly which probate or estate record names Caroline's father. Collection 4000201 'North Carolina, Rowan County Probate Records, 1753-1970' is name-searchable (personCount 289000). Per loc_001, the index is only ~40% complete; per the same quirk, full-text keyword search for 'Voss' (and variants such as Foss, Voas, or Vose) across the 1839-1900 window is more reliable than a name-only browse. Volume 004900301 (fulltextSearchable: true, 4,120 images, 40% indexed) supports that approach directly. Guardianship filings are included in the Rowan County probate series: if Caroline's father died before she reached majority (~1857), a guardian appointment would name her as the minor child and identify her deceased father — direct parentage evidence. Date range sized to the father's plausible lifespan: born roughly 1795-1815, he could have died any time from Caroline's birth (1839) to approximately 1900.

The 1850 US Federal Census names every household member individually with age and birthplace. Caroline was born 1839 and would be approximately 11 in 1850 — likely still living in her father's household before her ~1858 marriage. A Voss household in Rowan County containing a daughter named Caroline aged ~11 identifies the head of household as a candidate father, supplying his given name and approximate birth year. That name is then the identifier for confirming which Voss probate record (item 1) belongs to her father.

Fallback if the 1850 census returns no Voss household (the father may have died between 1839 and 1850). The 1840 US Federal Census was taken one year after Caroline's birth and names only the head of household, tallying other members by age-sex bracket. A Voss head of household in Rowan County with a female child under 5 documents a Voss patriarch in the county at Caroline's birth — consistent with that man being her father, even if the parentage link still requires corroboration from probate.

A parentage question requires a dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. Collection 4000202 'North Carolina, County Marriages, 1762-1979' is name-searchable (personCount 6240000). Searching for a Voss groom in Rowan County before 1839 (Caroline's birth year) would: (a) confirm a Voss couple as a unit; (b) supply the mother's given name, which census and death records usually omit; and (c) corroborate — by its date relative to Caroline's 1839 birth — a father otherwise identified only by census co-residence or a probate naming. Important limit: this marriage record establishes that the couple married; it does not by itself prove Caroline is their child — a separate record placing her with them (a census household or a probate naming her as heir) is still needed. Note also: the mother's surname on this record reflects her name at the time of this marriage only; whether it is her birth name or a prior married name remains open unless earlier records are found. Date range sized to the father's plausible marrying age (born ~1795-1815, likely marrying ~1815-1840).

Rowan County deed books sometimes record a father conveying land to a daughter or to her husband around the time of her marriage, naming the daughter with a parentage designation (e.g., 'to my daughter Caroline and her husband…'). The external_links_search returned a general Ancestry.com Rowan County landing page; neither collections_search nor volume_search identified a dedicated land-record collection for Rowan County on FamilySearch. Ancestry.com may carry digitized Rowan County deed books; original deed books are also held at the Rowan County Register of Deeds in Salisbury, NC. Date range sized to the father's land-owning years (born ~1795-1815) through Caroline's marriage era (~1858).

FAN cluster item — required for a parentage question. Once item 2 (1850 census) identifies the neighbors living adjacent to the Voss household, search collection 4000201 for those neighbors' probate records. Estate inventories, administrator's sale notices, and will appraisals routinely list buyers, witnesses, creditors, and appraisers from the surrounding community; adjoining landowners are named in deed boundary recitals and may recur in probate files. A neighbor's estate file mentioning the Voss family — or naming Caroline by relationship — would corroborate the parentage identified through items 1 and 2. This item is best executed after item 2 identifies the specific neighbors; date range sized to the plausible death years of neighbors found in the 1850 census, whose lifespans set this window.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Extract parent-naming fields from Patrick Flynn's 1908 PA death certificate**

Patrick's death cert (no. 4521, S3 in the project tree) is cited for the parent-child relationship with Thomas but its parent fields have never been extracted for q_001. Pennsylvania certificates from 1906+ have dedicated fields for father's name and mother's maiden name. This is the single most direct source already in hand — its parent entries will either confirm Thomas and reveal the mother, or expose gaps requiring further search. **Start here.**

**1880 US Federal Census — Thomas and Patrick Flynn, Schuylkill Co.**

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
County tax and exoneration lists for this period exist and are reachable via curated external links.

entry.rationale: The FamilySearch tree for Thomas Kerrigan (ZZKR-TH2) shows two candidate parents — Patrick Kerrigan (ZZKR-PA4, born ~1815 County Mayo, Ireland; died 1880 Pottsville) and Mary Gallagher (ZZKR-MG5, born ~1818 Ireland) — supported by a baptism source (SD-KER-BAP) recording Thomas's christening on 14 March 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville, and an 1850 census source (SD-KER-1850) showing Thomas, age 8, in Patrick and Mary's household. Neither source nor parent link is in the project tree. This plan extracts those two FS-tree sources, corroborates the parent-child link across subsequent censuses, searches for the parents' marriage record, Thomas's own marriage and burial records, Patrick's probate, naturalization records, and the FAN cluster identified by the baptism sponsors.

The FamilySearch tree (ZZKR-TH2) holds source SD-KER-BAP citing 'Pennsylvania, Catholic Church Records, 1750–1950' for Thomas's christening on 14 March 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville; the entry names father Patrick Kerrigan and mother Mary Gallagher, with baptismal sponsors John Gallagher and Bridget Kerrigan. The project tree carries no source and no parent link. Extracting this record's assertions is the single most direct step toward documenting the candidate parents — it is a sacramental register entry (original Catholic record), which is the primary parentage evidence in the absence of civil birth registration (loc_001: Pennsylvania civil registration did not begin until 1906). The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708–1985. Try variant spellings Carrigan and Corrigan if Kerrigan yields no hit.

The FamilySearch tree (ZZKR-TH2) holds a second source (SD-KER-1850) citing the 1850 United States Census for a household of Patrick Kerrigan, 35, laborer, born Ireland; Mary, 32, born Ireland; Thomas, 8, born Pennsylvania — in Pottsville, Schuylkill County. Thomas born in 1842 would be 8 in 1850, consistent with the baptism record. This is direct co-residence evidence placing Thomas in the household of the candidate parents. The project tree holds no source and no parent link. The FamilySearch tree ARK (SYNTH-KERRIGAN-1850) points directly to this record on FamilySearch. Ancestry also holds the 1850 Schuylkill County census (collection 1276, per external_links_search). Search first on FamilySearch; try Carrigan/Corrigan if Kerrigan yields no hit.

In 1860 Thomas was approximately 18 and may still be enumerated in Patrick and Mary's household, or beginning to appear independently nearby. United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181) is name-searchable (personCount 27,518,891). Searching for Patrick Kerrigan's household in Schuylkill County confirms the family's continued presence in Pottsville, provides Patrick's enumerated age and birthplace (corroborating the County Mayo, Ireland origin in the baptism record), and shows whether Thomas was still at home. Try Carrigan and Corrigan variants. If Thomas is not in Patrick's household, search for Thomas independently to document his location at age ~18.

By 1870 Thomas was approximately 28 and had formed his own household (daughter Bridget born 1871). Patrick (~55) and Mary (~52) would still be in Pottsville — Patrick died 1880. United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371). Searching both Patrick's and Thomas's households in Schuylkill County corroborates the parent-child link across two generations in the same locality, gives Patrick's age and birthplace one decade closer to his 1880 death, and locates Thomas in Pottsville before his marriage. Try Carrigan/Corrigan variants.

A dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate parents Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher to each other is required for a parentage question. Thomas was christened 14 March 1842, so their marriage preceded that date. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) and browse-only Church Records volume 007936751 (1842–1895, personCount 0) cover Schuylkill County Catholic registers. Because Patrick (born ~1815 County Mayo) and Mary (born ~1818 Ireland) emigrated from Ireland, their marriage may have occurred in Ireland before they arrived in Pennsylvania; if no Pennsylvania record is found, the fallback is County Mayo, Ireland Catholic records. The couple's marriage record supplies Mary's surname — Gallagher — as recorded in this marriage only; no remarriage is currently suspected, but if evidence emerges of a prior marriage for Mary, additional items should be added. Try Carrigan/Corrigan and Gallagher/Gallager variants.

Thomas married Ellen Burke; daughter Bridget was born in 1871 in Pottsville, placing the marriage approximately 1865–1871. Catholic marriage registers in Pennsylvania routinely name each party's age, birthplace, and sometimes parents' names, making this a potential source of parentage evidence for Thomas. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) is the primary search. The browse-only Marriage Records volume 007936753 (1870–1910, personCount 0) covers the later part of the window and should also be browsed if the indexed search yields nothing. Witnesses to the marriage are a FAN-cluster lead — a Kerrigan or Gallagher witness would corroborate the family network. Try Carrigan/Corrigan variants.

Patrick Kerrigan (born ~1815 County Mayo, Ireland) died in 1880 in Pottsville. A will, inventory, or letters of administration filed in Schuylkill County would name his heirs, potentially including Thomas, providing direct evidence of the father–son relationship. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0). The Schuylkill County Probate Records volume 007936749 (1851–1930, personCount 0) is also browse-only; browse the 1880–1888 portion. The date window is bounded by Patrick's own lifespan (born ~1815, died 1880) and a reasonable estate-settlement period — not by Thomas's research window.

Thomas died in 1898 in Pottsville. Pennsylvania civil death registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001 quirk), so no death certificate exists for this event. The burial register at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville — the parish where Thomas was christened in 1842 — may record his age at death, his parents' names, or his birthplace, all of which would corroborate or extend the parentage evidence from item 1. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) covers through 1985 and is the primary search. Try Carrigan/Corrigan if needed.

Thomas's 1842 baptism at St. Patrick's named John Gallagher and Bridget Kerrigan as sponsors — in Catholic practice, sponsors were typically relatives of the parents. John Gallagher (likely a brother or other kin of Mary Gallagher) and Bridget Kerrigan (likely a sister or other kin of Patrick Kerrigan) appearing in Schuylkill County census records near or alongside Patrick and Mary's household would corroborate the family networks behind both candidate parents. United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181, name-searchable, personCount 27,518,891) and 1870 (collection 1438024, name-searchable, personCount 38,558,371) are the primary searches. What this item reveals about Thomas is whether the named sponsors are documented as part of the Kerrigan or Gallagher family networks, thereby independently confirming the parents the baptism record asserts.

Patrick Kerrigan, born ~1815 in County Mayo, Ireland, emigrated before 1842 (Thomas was born in Pottsville that year). As an Irish immigrant settling in Pennsylvania, Patrick would have filed a declaration of intention and a petition for naturalization in Schuylkill County. Naturalization records routinely state the applicant's birthplace, birth year, and arrival date — corroborating Patrick's County Mayo origin asserted in the baptism record and confirming his identity as the father of Thomas. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records volume 007936750 (1849–1915, personCount 0) is browse-only; browse the 1849–1870 portion. The date window is bounded by Patrick's plausible naturalization years (he died 1880; naturalization most likely occurred within the first decade or two after arrival) — not by Thomas's research window.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly identified the FamilySearch profile for Thomas Kerrigan (ZZKR-TH2) and extracted the proposed parents Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher with their supporting sources (baptism 14 March 1842 at St. Patrick's Church naming both parents; 1850 census showing household co-residence). The plan treats this as a hypothesis to test rather than assumed fact, planning to extract and corroborate the attached sources first (items 1–2), then broaden with independent records (censuses, marriage, probate, naturalization, FAN cluster). All factual claims are grounded in the person_read response or the collections/volumes/external links searches. No fabricated material or unsupported assertions.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all requirements: (1) read the question person's FamilySearch profile and identified the proposed parents and their attached sources; (2) named what at least one source records (baptism naming both parents, 1850 census showing household); (3) created a plan that treats the pair as a hypothesis to test by extracting the attached records first, then corroborating with independent records; (4) kept the two trees apart by noting 'not in the project tree' and 'FamilySearch tree' explicitly. The plan is complete with 10 items covering church, census, probate, naturalization, and FAN records across the relevant time period.

This single clean recovery scores full credit per the retry policy.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: Every plan item's record_type matches the information need. Church records (items 1, 5, 6, 8) target sacramental registers for parentage, marriage, and burial evidence. Census records (items 2, 3, 4, 9) provide co-residence and corroboration across generations. Probate (item 7) targets heirs naming for father–son evidence. Naturalization (item 10) targets birthplace and arrival date corroboration. Each rationale explains why the type was chosen: e.g., item 1 states 'sacramental register entry (original Catholic record), which is the primary parentage evidence in the absence of civil birth registration'; item 7 states 'will, inventory, or letters of administration filed in Schuylkill County would name his heirs, potentially including Thomas, providing direct evidence of the father–son relationship.'

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Every item's rationale ties it to evidence about Thomas Kerrigan (the question's subject). Items 1–2 extract sources already attached to Thomas's profile. Items 3–4 search census records to corroborate Thomas's presence in Patrick's household across two generations. Item 5 searches for Patrick and Mary's marriage to establish the parental pair. Item 6 searches Thomas's own marriage record, which 'routinely name each party's age, birthplace, and sometimes parents' names, making this a potential source of parentage evidence for Thomas.' Item 7 targets Patrick's probate to name Thomas as heir. Item 8 searches Thomas's burial record for parentage information. Item 9 explicitly states 'What this item reveals about Thomas is whether the named sponsors are documented as part of the Kerrigan or Gallagher family networks, thereby independently confirming the parents the baptism record asserts.' Item 10 corroborates Patrick's identity as Thomas's father. No item pursues a relative's own record for its own sake.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: Sequence reflects defensible search order: items 1–2 extract the two attached FamilySearch sources (free, indexed, most direct evidence); items 3–4 broaden with subsequent censuses (free, indexed, narrow to Schuylkill County); item 5 searches for the parents' marriage (required for parentage question, date-bounded by Thomas's 1842 christening); item 6 searches Thomas's own marriage (1865–1871, bounded by daughter Bridget's 1871 birth); item 7 searches Patrick's probate (1880–1888, bounded by his death and settlement period); item 8 searches Thomas's burial (1898–1902, bounded by his 1898 death); item 9 searches FAN cluster (1850–1870 censuses, corroborating sponsors); item 10 searches Patrick's naturalization (1849–1870, bounded by plausible naturalization years). No item waits on evidence only a later item can produce. The date_ranges reach the later part of the question's window (Thomas's death 1898 is covered by item 8). Fallback for item 5 is explicitly noted: 'if no Pennsylvania record is found, the fallback is County Mayo, Ireland Catholic records.'
